name: Old Eko
blurb: The island where the city began: the palace, the cathedral, the first bridge and railway.

items.name: Iga Idunganran
items.text: The Oba of Lagos's palace. The first palace went up in 1670 for Oba Gabaro; the modern complex was commissioned on 1 October 1960. The name means roughly 'palace built on a pepper farm'.

items.name: Cathedral Church of Christ, Marina
items.text: Nigeria's oldest Anglican cathedral. The current Norman Gothic building, designed by Bagan Benjamin, was begun in 1924 and finished in 1946. Relics of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther were moved here in 1976.
items.source: Wikipedia: Cathedral Church of Christ, Lagos

items.name: Freedom Park
items.text: Site of Broad Street Prison, built in 1882 of mud and thatch, burned by opponents of colonial rule and rebuilt in 1885 with English bricks. Pulled down in 1979, it reopened as a memorial park for the 50th anniversary of independence.

items.name: Carter Bridge
items.text: The first link between Lagos Island and the mainland, opened in 1901 and named after Governor Gilbert Carter.

items.name: Iddo Terminus
items.text: Southern end of the Lagos–Ibadan railway, begun in 1896 and opened on 4 March 1901.

name: Brazilian Quarter
blurb: Returnees from slavery in Brazil rebuilt Lagos Island in an Afro-Brazilian style.

items.name: Campos Square
items.text: Heart of Popo Aguda, the quarter settled by the Agudas: Yoruba people freed from slavery in Bahia and Pernambuco who came back with Portuguese, Catholicism and building skills.

items.name: Shitta-Bey Mosque (approximate pin)
items.text: Afro-Brazilian mosque on Martins Street, designed by Brazilian architect João Baptista da Costa, completed in 1892 and opened in 1894. A National Monument since 2013.

items.name: Holy Cross Cathedral
items.text: Catholic cathedral at the edge of the Brazilian Quarter, one of the community's religious anchors alongside the Salvador Mosque.

name: Badagry slave route
blurb: The coastal town that was a major slave-trading port, and where missionaries built Nigeria's first storey building.

items.name: Seriki Williams Abass Slave Museum
items.text: Former barracoon of Chief Seriki Williams Abass. Around 40 cells once stood here, each holding up to 40 people; a couple survive, with shackles and chains on display.

items.name: Point of No Return, Gberefu (approximate pin)
items.text: On Gberefu Island, the last point enslaved people passed before being shipped out. Badagry's trade peaked between 1736 and 1789.

items.name: First Storey Building in Nigeria
items.text: Built by Church Missionary Society missionaries and regarded as the first storey building in Nigeria.
items.source: Wikipedia: First Storey Building in Nigeria

name: Independence era
blurb: The buildings of a new nation's capital.

items.name: Independence House
items.text: A 25-storey, 103 m office tower given by the British government for independence. Later called Defence House; partly burned in 1993.

items.name: National Stadium, Surulere
items.text: Opened 4 December 1972. Main venue of the 1973 All-Africa Games; 85,000 watched Nigeria beat Algeria 3–0 in the 1980 Nations Cup final here.

items.name: National Theatre, Iganmu
items.text: Finished in 1976 for FESTAC '77, built by Bulgaria's Techno Exportstroy on the design of the Palace of Culture and Sports in Varna. Rededicated in 2025 as the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and the Creative Arts.

items.name: Kalakuta Museum
items.text: The Ikeja house Fela rebuilt after soldiers burned the original Kalakuta Republic in Surulere on 18 February 1977. He lived here until 1997; it opened as a museum on his birthday, 15 October 2012.

items.name: New Afrika Shrine
items.text: Successor to the Afrika Shrine Fela founded in 1970, which burned in 1977. Run by Femi and Yeni Kuti; home of the yearly Felabration festival.

name: Water city
blurb: Lagos is built around a lagoon.

items.name: Makoko
items.text: A fishing settlement on stilts over the lagoon, settled in the 19th century. In July 2012 the state demolished stilt houses here, leaving nearly 3,000 people homeless.

items.name: Third Mainland Bridge
items.text: 11.8 km across the lagoon from Oworonshoki to Lagos Island. Africa's longest bridge until 1996.

items.name: Lekki Conservation Centre
items.text: Nature reserve founded by the Nigerian Conservation Foundation in 1990, with a canopy walkway about 400 m long.

name: The new edge
blurb: Land made from the sea, and the megaprojects of the Lekki corridor.

items.name: Eko Atlantic
items.text: A new district on about 10 km² of sand dredged in front of Bar Beach, which was eroding by about 30 m a year. An 8.5 km sea wall, the 'Great Wall of Lagos', protects it.

items.name: Lekki Deep Sea Port
items.text: Nigeria's first deep sea port, inaugurated 22 January 2023, with commercial operations from April 2023 and a 2.5 million TEU first phase.

items.name: Dangote Refinery
items.text: Commissioned 22 May 2023 on 6,180 acres in the Lekki Free Zone. Designed for 650,000 barrels a day; diesel and jet fuel from January 2024, petrol from September 2024.
